title: Purandar Under Jai Singh
subtitle: When Forts Became Bargaining Tables
era: Aurangzeb's first high-pressure Maratha campaign, March-June 1665
moral: A siege can end in terms that both sides use differently.

sources.citation: Mirza Raja Jai Singh's letters and Aurangzeb's farmans, cited in Jadunath Sarkar, Shivaji and His Times, 1973
Sabhasad Bakhar, c. 1697, and Jedhe Shakavali
sources.note: Near-contemporary Maratha records for Murarbaji, forts and treaty memory.

sources.citation: Niccolao Manucci, Storia do Mogor, trans. William Irvine, 1907-1908
sources.note: Contemporary European observer of Mughal-Maratha politics, not a siege eyewitness.

panels.shot: epic split-panel style wide, half showing a Mughal camp before Purandar, half a dim tent council

dialogue.text: In the summer of 1665, while Aurangzeb pressed the Deccan, Mirza Raja Jai Singh and Shivaji turned the storm around Purandar into a bargain that reshaped Maratha and Mughal power.

panels.shot: high aerial wide over the Deccan plateau

dialogue.text: Aurangzeb had just taken the Mughal throne. To tame the Deccan, he turned to Mirza Raja Jai Singh, the seasoned Rajput general, and pointed him toward Shivaji’s hill forts near Pune.

panels.shot: medium close on Jai Singh in his command tent

dialogue.text: In his letters to Aurangzeb, Jai Singh warned that Shivaji’s forts were the spine of Maratha power. The Rajput chose not a single glorious charge, but a careful net around those rocky citadels.

panels.shot: ground-level wide of multiple fort lines

dialogue.text: By March 1665, Mughal detachments moved like fingers into the Sahyadri hills. Jai Singh’s plan, recorded in his dispatches, was to isolate Purandar by taking its satellite posts one by one.

panels.shot: interior medium of Shivaji in Purandar council

dialogue.text: Within Purandar, Shivaji weighed each move. Sabhasad’s Bakhar remembers his words to Murarbaji Deshpande: hold the fort, bleed the enemy, and buy time while he gauged Jai Singh’s true intent.

panels.shot: low-angle wide from Mughal trenches looking up at Purandar

dialogue.text: The Mughal records speak of trenches dug, batteries raised, and supplies hauled up under fire. This was not a raider’s skirmish, but slow, grinding siege craft brought to the Deccan hills.

panels.shot: dynamic mid-action wide on Murarbaji leading a sortie

dialogue.text: Sabhasad paints Murarbaji as the storm of Purandar, leading furious sorties down the slopes. For weeks his small bands harried Mughal trenches, making every yard of ground costlier.

panels.shot: close three-quarter on Jai Singh observing battlefield from a rise

dialogue.text: Jai Singh’s letters do not dwell on Murarbaji, but they note stout resistance. The Rajput commander pressed on, bringing fresh contingents, adjusting routes, closing every path that might relieve Purandar.

panels.shot: intense mid-shot skirmish on the slopes below Purandar

dialogue.text: Accounts differ on each assault, but they agree on this: in a fierce fight on Purandar’s lower works, Murarbaji fell. His death broke the fort’s fiercest edge, even as his name entered Maratha memory.

panels.shot: somber interior medium on Shivaji receiving news

dialogue.text: Jedhe Shakavali notes the loss of Purandar’s commander. Shivaji, hearing of Murarbaji’s end and the tightening ring, now faced a choice between heroic ruin and a bargain on harsh terms.

panels.shot: medium inside Jai Singh's tent as an envoy bows

dialogue.text: Around this time, talks began. Mughal dispatches present Jai Singh as the calm victor offering terms; Maratha bakhars remember Shivaji as the strategist, bargaining to save his core strength.

panels.shot: tight interior wide of the first face-to-face meeting

dialogue.text: Raja Jai Singh: "Let us make such peace that neither throne need fear the other’s shadow."

panels.shot: medium close on Shivaji listening, half-profile of Jai Singh

dialogue.text: European observer Manucci later wrote of Jai Singh’s skill with words. Yet each side’s chroniclers lay the credit at their own hero’s feet, a reminder that treaties are stories as much as signatures.

panels.shot: diagrammatic overhead-style wide of forts being marked on a map

dialogue.text: The Purandar treaty of June 1665 is clear: Shivaji ceded 23 forts to the empire, retained 12, agreed to serve in person, and saw his son Sambhaji enter the Mughal ranks as a mansabdar.

panels.shot: exterior wide of Mughal flag over surrendered outwork, distant forts still Maratha

dialogue.text: Imperial farmans praised Jai Singh’s success: Purandar’s fall, forts yielded, a troublesome power brought to heel. For Aurangzeb, it was a step toward a firmer Deccan frontier under imperial colors.

panels.shot: quiet interior medium on Shivaji with his close followers

dialogue.text: Shivaji: "We yield stone to save strength. The hills will wait for our return."

panels.shot: medium on Jai Singh writing a dispatch by lamplight

dialogue.text: In his report, Jai Singh urged Aurangzeb to keep this new balance, to use Shivaji’s loyalty rather than drive him back to rebellion. His concern was not only conquest, but a workable settlement.

panels.shot: time-lapse style wide, Purandar in changing light

dialogue.text: Later events would shatter this fragile peace. Yet in 1665, Purandar had shown that a fort could fall not only to cannon, but to negotiation, each side believing it had outplayed the other.

panels.shot: paired close-ups, split frame of Jai Singh and Shivaji looking in opposite directions

dialogue.text: Purandar under Jai Singh stands as a moment when siege turned into diplomacy, and when both a Rajput general and a Maratha king used the same treaty as a step toward very different futures.
